opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so LIMA was definitely a big inspiration for us. The core insight there was that most of a model's knowledge and capabilities come from pretraining, and alignment or fine-tuning is mostly about teaching the model a format or a style of interaction. They showed you could get really strong chat behavior from just about a thousand carefully curated examples.

With s1, our question was basically: does the same thing hold for reasoning? If the base model, in our case Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, has already seen a huge amount of math and scientific reasoning during pretraining, then maybe you don't need hundreds of thousands of reasoning traces and big reinforcement learning pipelines. Maybe you just need a small set of high-quality examples to unlock that latent ability and show the model how to think step by step at length.

So we started from a much larger pool, roughly 59,000 questions, and then filtered down to 1,000 using three criteria. The first was quality: we removed examples with formatting issues or problems in the data. The second was difficulty: we wanted problems that were genuinely hard, so we used signals like whether smaller models could already solve them and how long the reasoning traces were. If a problem was easy, it wasn't going to teach the model much. The third was diversity: we made sure to cover many different domains, different areas of math and also science, so the model wouldn't overfit to one type of problem.

What was interesting is that we ran ablations, and each criterion mattered. If you only selected randomly, or only for difficulty, or only for diversity, performance dropped compared to combining all three. And training on the full 59K pool gave only marginal gains over the 1K set while costing a lot more compute. So in a sense, the LIMA hypothesis held up quite well for reasoning: a small, carefully chosen set was enough, and then we paired that with budget forcing at test time to actually control how much the model thinks.

r001.rationale: The response says LIMA showed strong chat behavior could be achieved with about a thousand carefully curated examples, expressing the small-data alignment hypothesis.

r002.rationale: It explicitly frames the s1 question as whether LIMA’s small-data approach also holds for reasoning, motivating the choice of 1,000 reasoning examples.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, LIMA was definitely a big inspiration for us. The core idea there was that if you take a strong pretrained base model, you really don't need tens of thousands of instruction examples to get it to behave like a good assistant. A thousand carefully chosen examples get you most of the way, because the capabilities are already in the model and you're mostly just teaching it a format, a style, surfacing what's already there.

So when we started s1, our question was essentially: does the same thing hold for reasoning? Everyone was assuming you needed enormous amounts of reasoning data, hundreds of thousands of chains of thought, or a big RL run. We wanted to test the minimal version. If we pick a thousand really good questions with reasoning traces, can we elicit test-time scaling and strong reasoning performance from a base model like Qwen2.5-32B?

The thing that mattered a lot was how we picked those thousand. We started with a pool of around 59,000 questions and filtered on three things. First, quality, so we threw out anything with formatting issues, broken traces, that sort of thing. Second, difficulty, where we checked whether existing models could already solve the question easily, and if they could, we dropped it, because an easy example doesn't teach the model much. We also used the length of the reasoning trace as a proxy for how hard a problem is. And third, diversity, so we spread the examples across many domains, math, physics, chemistry, and so on, rather than just loading up on one competition math distribution.

And what we found really mirrored LIMA. Training on all 59K didn't give you much over the carefully selected 1K. But randomly selecting 1K, or selecting only on diversity, or only on difficulty, was clearly worse than combining all three. So the sample efficiency is real, but it's not free, you have to be deliberate about the data.

The other half of the story, which LIMA didn't have, was the test-time side. We added this budget forcing trick where you can suppress the model from stopping and append "Wait" to make it keep thinking, or cut it off early. That's what lets you actually scale compute at inference and see performance go up. So I'd say the 1K data gets the reasoning behavior out of the model, and budget forcing gives you control over how much it reasons. The combination is what made the whole thing work with such a small amount of training.

r001.rationale: The response says a strong pretrained model needs relatively few carefully chosen examples to behave like an assistant, because training mainly teaches format and style and surfaces existing capabilities.

r002.rationale: It explicitly presents the 1,000-example s1 experiment as asking whether LIMA’s small-data result also holds for reasoning.

astra-6.text:
We took LIMA’s central idea—that a small amount of high-quality data can be enough to elicit capabilities the model already has—and asked whether that also applies to reasoning. Rather than simply adding more examples, we focused on which examples would make those thousand count.

We thought about three things: quality, difficulty, and diversity. You want reliable solutions, problems that require meaningful reasoning, and enough variety that the model isn’t just learning one narrow pattern. The idea wasn’t that a thousand examples would teach a model all of reasoning from scratch. It was that, with a strong pretrained model, a carefully selected set might be enough to bring out its reasoning capabilities.

r001.rationale: It describes LIMA’s idea as using a small amount of high-quality data to elicit capabilities the model already has, conveying that alignment can use relatively little training data.

r002.rationale: It says they asked whether LIMA’s small-data idea applies to reasoning and discusses selecting 1,000 reasoning examples for that purpose.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea we took from LIMA was that a small amount of carefully selected data can be enough to bring out capabilities the model already has. So rather than trying to collect as many reasoning examples as possible, we focused on selecting 1,000 good ones.

We looked at three things: difficulty, diversity, and quality. We wanted problems that required real reasoning, a range of problems so the model wouldn’t just learn one narrow pattern, and solutions that were correct and useful to learn from. The hypothesis was that the base model already had a lot of the underlying knowledge, and these examples could teach it how to use that knowledge in a reasoning response.

I wouldn’t interpret that as saying 1,000 is some universally optimal number. It was a way to test how far careful data selection could take us with a very small training set.

r001.rationale: It says a small amount of data can bring out existing capabilities, but does not clearly state that model alignment itself requires relatively little training data.

r002.rationale: It presents the 1,000 examples as a test of how far LIMA’s small-data approach could go for reasoning, emphasizing careful selection over collecting more examples.
